Pillar
PIL-'r
n. (rendering Hebrew 'ammūd and matstsebah, Greek stulos)
From Old French piler, from Latin pila, a pier or column. Hebrew distinguishes two things the English word merges: 'ammūd is a structural column that stands and bears weight, from 'āmad, to stand; matstsebah is a standing stone set up as a memorial or witness. The distinction matters, since Scripture commends the one and repeatedly condemns the other when it is raised to a false god.

Biblical Definition

A pillar in Scripture is something that stands and makes others stand, and God takes the figure to Himself in the wilderness: “And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night” (Exo 13:21) — a column of God's own presence, giving shade in the day and light in the dark, and moving so that Israel's marching orders were visible to every man in the camp. Against that stands the pillar a soul becomes when it refuses to move: “But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt” (Gen 19:26) — a monument to a heart that had left Sodom in body only, and the Lord Jesus made her a warning to His own disciples in one sentence: remember Lot's wife. The word is then applied to the church, and the metaphor assigns it a definite office: “the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15). A pillar does not generate what it holds; it displays and upholds it, which is exactly the church's relation to truth she did not invent. Men may be pillars too, and Paul names three without flattery: “James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars” (Gal 2:9). And the promise to the overcomer takes the figure into permanence: “Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out” (Rev 3:12) — spoken to the church at Philadelphia in a region whose cities were shaken by earthquakes and whose people repeatedly fled them.

Webster 1828 Definition

A column or upright support; a standing stone set up as a memorial; and in Scripture the pillar of cloud and fire that led Israel, the pillar of salt Lot's wife became, the church as the pillar and ground of the truth, and the pillar the overcomer is made in God's temple.

expand to see more

PILLAR, n. 1. A kind of irregular column, round and insulated, used to support or adorn a building.

2. A supporter; that which sustains or upholds; that on which some superstructure rests.

3. A monument raised to commemorate a person or event; a standing stone.

4. In Hebrew, from a root signifying to stand; that which stands and causes to stand.

5. In Scripture, a pillar of a cloud, a pillar of fire. Exod. 13. The pillar and ground of the truth. 1 Tim. 3.

Key Scripture

Exodus 13:21 — "And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night:"

Genesis 19:26 — "But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt."

1 Timothy 3:15 — "But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth."

Revelation 3:12 — "Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God: and I will write upon him my new name."

Modern Corruption

The church is made the source of truth rather than its support, so that her pronouncements are treated as generating what they were given to uphold; and at the other extreme her office as pillar is denied altogether in favour of a purely private religion.

expand to see more

1Ti 3:15 is the classic proof text of Roman claims for the magisterium: because the church is the pillar and ground of the truth, it is argued that her teaching office is the truth's foundation and guarantor, so that Scripture depends on the church for its authority and the church may add to it. The metaphor itself refutes the inference. A pillar does not produce the building it holds, and nothing is truer for being displayed on a column. The church's office is to hold up, exhibit, and guard what she has received — the faith once delivered unto the saints, which she may not add to and may not amend. The Bereans were commended for testing an apostle's preaching by the Scriptures, which would be impossible if the teaching body were the standard rather than the servant of the standard.

The opposite corruption discards the office entirely. Where Christianity is treated as a private matter between the individual and God, the visible church becomes optional, and the truth is left with no appointed upholder in the world. Scripture assumes otherwise everywhere: elders are charged to hold fast the faithful word, to convince the gainsayers, and to commit what they have heard to faithful men who shall be able to teach others also. The principle to recover is the exact relation the figure sets: Scripture is the truth, the church is the pillar, and a pillar that carries nothing has failed as surely as one that claims to have made the roof. The promise of Rev 3:12 is the personal form of the same thing — the overcomer himself made a fixture in God's temple, who shall go no more out.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'ammūd is a structural column, from 'āmad, to stand; matstsebah is a standing stone or memorial pillar, condemned when raised to false gods. Greek stulos is a pillar or column.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'ammūd (H5982) — a column or pillar that bears weight; from 'āmad, to stand; used of the pillar of cloud and of the temple columns.

Hebrew matstsebah (H4676) — a standing stone set up as memorial or witness; Jacob's pillar at Bethel (Gen 28:18), and the images Israel was commanded to break down.

Hebrew n'tsīb (H5333) — a pillar or garrison, that which is set up; the word for the pillar of salt in Gen 19:26.

Greek stulos (G4769) — a pillar or column; the pillar and ground of the truth (1Ti 3:15), and the pillar in the temple of God (Rev 3:12).

Greek hedraiōma (G1477) — a stay, support, or ground; paired with stulos in 1Ti 3:15 to describe the church's office.

Usage

"Of God's guiding presence: the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud... and by night in a pillar of fire (Exo 13:21)."

"Of the church's office: the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth (1Ti 3:15)."

"Of the overcomer's permanence: him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God (Rev 3:12)."
